claim: TRIP8b binding to the CNBD of mammalian HCN channels prevents their regulation by cAMP.
source: Binding of TRIP8b to the cyclic nucleotide binding domain (CNBD) of mammalian hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels prevents their regulation by cAMP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact that forms the basis for the study.

claim: TRIP8b is expressed exclusively in the brain.
source: Since TRIP8b is expressed exclusively in the brain, we envisage that it can be used for orthogonal control of HCN channels beyond the central nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A 40-aa long peptide (TRIP8bnano) recapitulates affinity and gating effects of TRIP8b in HCN isoforms (hHCN1, mHCN2, rbHCN4).
source: To this end, we have identified by rational design a 40-aa long peptide (TRIP8bnano) that recapitulates affinity and gating effects of TRIP8b in HCN isoforms (hHCN1, mHCN2, rbHCN4) and in the cardiac current If in rabbit and mouse sinoatrial node cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: TRIP8bnano recapitulates affinity and gating effects of TRIP8b in the cardiac current If in rabbit and mouse sinoatrial node cardiomyocytes.
source: To this end, we have identified by rational design a 40-aa long peptide (TRIP8bnano) that recapitulates affinity and gating effects of TRIP8b in HCN isoforms (hHCN1, mHCN2, rbHCN4) and in the cardiac current If in rabbit and mouse sinoatrial node cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: TAT-TRIP8bnano successfully prevented β-adrenergic activation of mouse If leaving the stimulation of the L-type calcium current (ICaL) unaffected.
source: Guided by an NMR-derived structural model that identifies the key molecular interactions between TRIP8bnano and the HCN CNBD, we further designed a cell-penetrating peptide (TAT-TRIP8bnano) which successfully prevented β-adrenergic activation of mouse If leaving the stimulation of the L-type calcium current (ICaL) unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: TRIP8bnano represents a novel approach to selectively control HCN activation.
source: TRIP8bnano represents a novel approach to selectively control HCN activation, which yields the promise of a more targeted pharmacology compared to pore blockers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: HCN channels are the molecular correlate of the If/Ih current.
source: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN1-4) channels are the molecular correlate of the If/Ih current, which plays a key role in controlling several higher order physiological functions, including dendritic integration and intrinsic rhythmicity both in cardiac and neuronal cells (Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: If/Ih current plays a key role in controlling dendritic integration and intrinsic rhythmicity in cardiac and neuronal cells.
source: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN1-4) channels are the molecular correlate of the If/Ih current, which plays a key role in controlling several higher order physiological functions, including dendritic integration and intrinsic rhythmicity both in cardiac and neuronal cells (Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: HCN channels are modulated by the direct binding of cAMP to their cyclic nucleotide binding domain (CNBD).
source: Unique among the voltage-gated ion channel superfamily, HCN channels are modulated by the direct binding of cAMP to their cyclic nucleotide binding domain (CNBD).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Binding of cAMP increases the channel open probability upon hyperpolarization via conformational changes in the CNBD that are propagated to the pore through the C-linker domain.
source: Binding of the cyclic nucleotide increases the channel open probability upon hyperpolarization via conformational changes in the CNBD that are propagated to the pore through the C-linker domain (DiFrancesco and Tortora, 1991; Wainger et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: TRIP8b is a brain-specific auxiliary (β) subunit that modulates HCN channel trafficking and gating.
source: In addition to cAMP, HCN channels are regulated by TRIP8b, a brain-specific auxiliary (β) subunit, which modulates two independent features of the channel, namely trafficking and gating (Santoro et al., 2009; Zolles et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: TRIP8b binds HCN channels through two distinct sites: the TPR domain and the TRIP8bcore domain.
source: For this dual regulation, TRIP8b binds HCN channels through two distinct sites: via the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain, which interacts with the last three amino acids (SNL) of HCN channels and regulates their trafficking; and via the TRIP8bcore domain, which interacts with the CNBD and antagonizes the effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of the channel (Santoro et al., 2011; Han et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The TPR domain of TRIP8b interacts with the last three amino acids (SNL) of HCN channels and regulates their trafficking.
source: For this dual regulation, TRIP8b binds HCN channels through two distinct sites: via the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain, which interacts with the last three amino acids (SNL) of HCN channels and regulates their trafficking; and via the TRIP8bcore domain, which interacts with the CNBD and antagonizes the effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of the channel (Santoro et al., 2011; Han et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The TRIP8bcore domain interacts with the CNBD and antagonizes the effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of the channel.
source: For this dual regulation, TRIP8b binds HCN channels through two distinct sites: via the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain, which interacts with the last three amino acids (SNL) of HCN channels and regulates their trafficking; and via the TRIP8bcore domain, which interacts with the CNBD and antagonizes the effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of the channel (Santoro et al., 2011; Han et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: cAMP-dependent modulation of HCN channels underlies distinct roles of cAMP in heart rate regulation.
source: cAMP-dependent modulation of HCN channels underlies distinct roles of cAMP in heart rate regulation (DiFrancesco, 1993) and development of peripheral neuropathic pain (Emery et al., 2012; Herrmann et al., 2017), which can be dissected by using a TRIP8b-based tool.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: cAMP-dependent modulation of HCN channels underlies development of peripheral neuropathic pain.
source: cAMP-dependent modulation of HCN channels underlies distinct roles of cAMP in heart rate regulation (DiFrancesco, 1993) and development of peripheral neuropathic pain (Emery et al., 2012; Herrmann et al., 2017), which can be dissected by using a TRIP8b-based tool.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Peptide-based drugs (2–50 aa long) open new therapeutic possibilities with an advantage over small molecules in terms of specificity and affinity for the target.
source: In this regard, peptide-based drugs (2–50 aa long) are emerging as a fascinating application area as they open new therapeutic possibilities with an advantage over small molecules in terms of specificity and affinity for the target (Fosgerau and Hoffmann, 2015; Henninot et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: TRIP8bcore (80 aa long) interacts with the HCN CNBD and prevents cAMP modulation in full length channels.
source: In previous studies, we identified the core portion of TRIP8b (TRIP8bcore, 80 aa long) that interacts with the HCN CNBD and prevents cAMP modulation in full length channels (Santoro et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013; Saponaro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors with citations to support it.

claim: A 37 aa peptide identified by Lyman et al. (2017) failed to reproduce the binding affinity of TRIP8bcore.
source: A recent paper (Lyman et al., 2017) reported an even shorter binding sequence of TRIP8b (37 aa). However, this peptide, which was identified by progressive truncation of TRIP8bcore, failed to reproduce the binding affinity of the starting construct.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Evidence for activity of the 37 aa peptide identified by Lyman et al. (2017) on HCN currents is lacking.
source: Moreover, evidence for activity of this peptide on HCN currents is lacking.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the cited study.

claim: TRIP8bcore interacts with two elements of the isolated CNBD protein fragment from HCN channels: the C-helix and the N-bundle loop.
source: We have previously shown that TRIP8bcore (residues 223–303 of mouse TRIP8b splice variant 1a4, hereafter TRIP8b) interacts with two elements of the isolated CNBD protein fragment from HCN channels (residues 521–672 of human HCN2, hereafter CNBD): the C-helix and the N-bundle loop, a sequence connecting helix E' of the C-linker with helix A of the CNBD (Saponaro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors with a citation to support it.

claim: Each of the N-bundle loop and C-helix is necessary but not sufficient for TRIP8bcore binding to CNBD.
source: Biochemical assays confirmed that each of these two elements, that is, the N-bundle loop and C-helix, is necessary but not sufficient for binding (Saponaro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors with a citation to support it.

claim: TRIP8bnano comprises residues 235–275 of TRIP8b.
source: We thus identified a 40-aa peptide (TRIP8bnano, comprising residues 235–275 of TRIP8b, Figure 1A) with a binding KD of 1.5 ± 0.1 µM, a value similar to the KD of 1.2 ± 0.1 µM obtained with TRIP8bcore (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TRIP8bnano has a binding KD of 1.5 ± 0.1 µM for CNBD.
source: We thus identified a 40-aa peptide (TRIP8bnano, comprising residues 235–275 of TRIP8b, Figure 1A) with a binding KD of 1.5 ± 0.1 µM, a value similar to the KD of 1.2 ± 0.1 µM obtained with TRIP8bcore (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRIP8bcore has a binding KD of 1.2 ± 0.1 µM for CNBD.
source: We thus identified a 40-aa peptide (TRIP8bnano, comprising residues 235–275 of TRIP8b, Figure 1A) with a binding KD of 1.5 ± 0.1 µM, a value similar to the KD of 1.2 ± 0.1 µM obtained with TRIP8bcore (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRIP8bnano folds upon interaction with the CNBD.
source: The comparison of the 1H-15N HSQC spectra of TRIP8bnano with and without CNBD bound shows that the peptide folds upon interaction with the CNBD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectroscopy as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TRIP8bnano displays two α-helices (stretch L238-E250 named helix N and stretch T253-R269 named helix C) when bound to CNBD.
source: The φ and ψ dihedral angles obtained from the NMR assignment indicate that the peptide displays two α-helices (stretch L238-E250 named helix N and stretch T253-R269 named helix C) when bound to CNBD.
evidence: This is determined from NMR data as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three and six residues at the N- and C- termini of TRIP8bnano, respectively, are unstructured when bound to CNBD.
source: The helices are separated by two amino acids; three and six residues at the N- and C- termini, respectively, are unstructured (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is determined from NMR data as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The interaction with TRIP8bnano does not affect the overall fold of the CNBD.
source: NMR-analysis of the CNBD fragment bound to TRIP8bnano revealed that the interaction with the peptide does not affect the overall fold of the protein.
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis.

claim: The CNBD adopts the typical fold of the cAMP-free state when bound to TRIP8bnano.
source: Thus, the CNBD adopts the typical fold of the cAMP-free state, in line with previous evidence that this is the form bound by TRIP8b (Saponaro et al., 2014; DeBerg et al., 2015)
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: TRIP8bnano binding to the CNBD induces a well-defined secondary structure of the distal region of the C-helix.
source: Indeed, our results show that TRIP8bnano binding to the CNBD induces a well-defined secondary structure of the distal region of the C-helix (Figure 2).
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distal region of the C-helix (residues 657–662) is unstructured in the free form of the CNBD.
source: This means that the distal region of the C-helix (residues 657–662), which is unstructured in the free form of the CNBD (Saponaro et al., 2014; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017), extends into a helical structure upon ligand binding irrespectively of whether the ligand is cAMP (Puljung and Zagotta, 2013; Saponaro et al., 2014; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017) or TRIP8b (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The distal region of the C-helix extends into a helical structure upon binding of either cAMP or TRIP8b.
source: This means that the distal region of the C-helix (residues 657–662), which is unstructured in the free form of the CNBD (Saponaro et al., 2014; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017), extends into a helical structure upon ligand binding irrespectively of whether the ligand is cAMP (Puljung and Zagotta, 2013; Saponaro et al., 2014; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017) or TRIP8b (Figure 2).
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis and comparison with previous studies.

claim: TRIP8bnano binding to the CNBD does not induce P-helix formation.
source: In contrast, and very differently from cAMP, which directly contacts the P-helix in the Phosphate Binding cassette (PBC) and causes its folding (Saponaro et al., 2014; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017), the NMR data show that TRIP8bnano binding to the CNBD does not induce P-helix formation (Figure 2).
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis as shown in Figure 2.

claim: cAMP directly contacts the P-helix in the Phosphate Binding cassette (PBC) and causes its folding.
source: In contrast, and very differently from cAMP, which directly contacts the P-helix in the Phosphate Binding cassette (PBC) and causes its folding (Saponaro et al., 2014; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017), the NMR data show that TRIP8bnano binding to the CNBD does not induce P-helix formation (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: TRIP8bnano binds to both the C-helix and the N-bundle loop of the CNBD.
source: Scrutiny of the model shows that TRIP8bnano binds to both the C-helix and the N-bundle loop (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the structural model in Figure 3A.

claim: Binding of TRIP8bnano to the C-helix is mainly guided by electrostatic interactions between the negative charges on TRIP8bnano and the positive charges on the CNBD.
source: Binding to the C-helix is mainly guided by electrostatic interactions between the negative charges on TRIP8bnano, and the positive charges on the CNBD (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the structural model in Figure 3A.

claim: K665 and K666 of CNBD form a double saline bridge with E265 and E264 of TRIP8bnano.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the model highlights a double saline bridge (K665 and K666 of CNBD with E265 and E264 of TRIP8bnano) in line with the ITC results described above (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in the structural model in Figure 3B and validated by ITC experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reverse charge mutations K665E or K666E (CNBD) strongly reduced the CNBD/TRIP8bnano binding affinity.
source: As expected, reverse charge mutations K665E or K666E (CNBD) as well as E264K or E265K (TRIP8bnano) each strongly reduced the CNBD/TRIP8bnano binding affinity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reverse charge mutations E264K or E265K (TRIP8bnano) strongly reduced the CNBD/TRIP8bnano binding affinity.
source: As expected, reverse charge mutations K665E or K666E (CNBD) as well as E264K or E265K (TRIP8bnano) each strongly reduced the CNBD/TRIP8bnano binding affinity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Upon folding of the distal portion of the C-helix, the side chains of residues R662 and K665 face to the inside when contacting cAMP, but face to the outside when binding TRIP8b.
source: Our modeling data suggest that, upon folding of the distal portion of the C-helix, the side chains of residues R662 and K665 face to the inside when contacting cAMP, but face to the outside when binding TRIP8b (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in the structural model in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: cAMP and TRIP8b directly compete for the binding to the distal region of C-helix.
source: This indicates that cAMP and TRIP8b directly compete for the binding to the distal region of C-helix.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model showing that both ligands interact with the same residues.

claim: R650 in the proximal portion of the CNBD C-helix contacts E240 and E241 in helix N of TRIP8bnano.
source: In addition to clarifying the role of residues in the distal portion of the CNBD C-helix, the model also highlights a second important cluster of electrostatic interactions, with R650 in the proximal portion of the CNBD C-helix contacting E240 and E241 in helix N of TRIP8bnano (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the structural model in Figure 3C.

claim: R650E caused a more than six-fold reduction in binding affinity for TRIP8bnano.
source: The results in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 show that R650E caused a more than six-fold reduction in binding affinity for TRIP8bnano, with smaller but significant effects seen also for E240R and E241R.
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: E240R and E241R mutations caused smaller but significant reductions in binding affinity for CNBD.
source: The results in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 show that R650E caused a more than six-fold reduction in binding affinity for TRIP8bnano, with smaller but significant effects seen also for E240R and E241R.
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: N547 in the N-bundle loop of the CNBD interacts with D252 in the link between helix N and helix C of TRIP8bnano.
source: A third important contact highlighted by the model is the interaction between N547 in the N-bundle loop of the CNBD and D252 in the link between helix N and helix C of TRIP8bnano (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in the structural model in Figure 3D.

claim: N547D greatly reduced binding to TRIP8bnano.
source: As predicted, N547D greatly reduced binding to TRIP8b in ITC assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), with a smaller but significant effect observed also for D252N (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: D252N caused a smaller but significant reduction in binding to CNBD.
source: As predicted, N547D greatly reduced binding to TRIP8b in ITC assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), with a smaller but significant effect observed also for D252N (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured by ITC as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The N-bundle loop contributes in a substantial manner to the binding of TRIP8b.
source: These results confirm and extend our previous finding that the N-bundle loop contributes in a substantial manner to the binding of TRIP8b (Saponaro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is confirmed by the mutagenesis data and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The affinity of the N547D CNBD mutant for cAMP is much lower than that of the wild type.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, the affinity of the mutant is much lower than that of the wt (N547D KD = 5.5 ± 0.4 µM (n = 3) vs. wt KD = 1.4 ± 0.1 µM (n = 3)).
evidence: This is measured by ITC.

claim: Addition of 5 μM cAMP caused a right shift in the V1/2 of the N547D mutant HCN2 channel of only 5 mV while the wt channel shifted by 12 mV.
source: Moreover, we measured a reduced sensitivity to cAMP also in patch clamp experiments where addition of 5 μM cAMP caused a right shift in the V1/2 of the mutant HCN2 channel of only 5 mV while the wt channel shifted by 12 mV (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The N547D CNBD mutant is appropriately folded.
source: To exclude that the N547D mutation affects the overall structure of the CNBD, we performed the NMR (1H-15N HSQC spectrum) analysis of the N547D CNBD mutant. Our data show that the protein is appropriately folded (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is determined by NMR analysis as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The N-bundle loop allosterically modulates cAMP binding to the CNBD.
source: In conclusion, since the N-bundle loop does not directly contact any of the residues of the cAMP binding pocket, these findings underscore a previously unaddressed role of the N-bundle loop in allosterically modulating cAMP binding to the CNBD (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that N547D affects cAMP binding without directly contacting the cAMP binding pocket.

claim: TRIP8bnano prevents the cAMP-induced right shift in V1/2 of about 13 mV in HCN4.
source: The addition of TRIP8bnano prevents the cAMP-induced right shift of about 13 mV in HCN4 (V1/2 = -102.8, –89.2, −102.1 mV, for control, cAMP and cAMP + TRIP8bnano, respectively), and of about 11 mV in HCN2 (V1/2 = -93.7, –83.5, −94.5 mV, for control, cAMP and cAMP + TRIP8bnano, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4.

claim: TRIP8bnano prevents the cAMP-induced right shift in V1/2 of about 11 mV in HCN2.
source: The addition of TRIP8bnano prevents the cAMP-induced right shift of about 13 mV in HCN4 (V1/2 = -102.8, –89.2, −102.1 mV, for control, cAMP and cAMP + TRIP8bnano, respectively), and of about 11 mV in HCN2 (V1/2 = -93.7, –83.5, −94.5 mV, for control, cAMP and cAMP + TRIP8bnano, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4.

claim: In HCN1, TRIP8bnano induced a left shift in V1/2 of about 10 mV (from – 72.8 to −82 mV).
source: In HCN1, TRIP8bnano induced a left shift in V1/2 of about 10 mV (from – 72.8 to −82 mV) which is comparable to that induced by the R549E mutation (from −72.7 to −80.4 mV) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4.

claim: The R549E mutation in HCN1 induced a left shift in V1/2 from −72.7 to −80.4 mV.
source: In HCN1, TRIP8bnano induced a left shift in V1/2 of about 10 mV (from – 72.8 to −82 mV) which is comparable to that induced by the R549E mutation (from −72.7 to −80.4 mV) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRIP8bnano peptide affects channel gating only if added to the intracellular solution.
source: The V1/2 value, which is similar to that of cAMP alone (−91.7 vs. −89.2 mV), confirmed that TRIP8bnano peptide affects channel gating only if added to the intracellular solution presumably because it does not diffuse through the cell membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by a control experiment where TRIP8bnano was added to the extracellular medium.

claim: TRIP8bnano prevents the acceleration of activation kinetics induced by cAMP in HCN channels.
source: It is worth noting that TRIP8bnano prevents other related effects of cAMP activation in HCN channels, such as the acceleration of activation kinetics (Wainger et al., 2001) and, for HCN2 only, the increase in maximal current (Chen et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch clamp experiments and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: TRIP8bnano prevents the increase in maximal current induced by cAMP in HCN2.
source: It is worth noting that TRIP8bnano prevents other related effects of cAMP activation in HCN channels, such as the acceleration of activation kinetics (Wainger et al., 2001) and, for HCN2 only, the increase in maximal current (Chen et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The activation kinetics (τon) of HCN4 measured at −120 mV was: control = 2 ± 0.2 s, 1 μM cAMP = 1.2 ± 0.1 s, 1 μM cAMP + 10 μM TRIP8bnano = 2 ± 0.3 s.
source: For example, the activation kinetics (τon) of HCN4 measured at −120 mV was: control = 2 ± 0.2 s, 1 μM cAMP = 1.2 ± 0.1 s, 1 μM cAMP + 10 μM TRIP8bnano = 2 ± 0.3 s (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: If is a key contributor of the diastolic depolarization phase of the pacemaker action potential cycle in SAN myocytes.
source: In these cells, If is key contributor of the diastolic depolarization phase of the pacemaker action potential cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The autonomic nervous system modulates the frequency of action potential firing in SAN myocytes by changing intracellular cAMP levels, which in turn acts on f-HCN channel open probability.
source: Moreover, the autonomic nervous system modulates the frequency of action potential firing by changing intracellular cAMP levels, which in turn acts on f-HCN channel open probability (DiFrancesco, 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: The averaged If activation curve measured in presence of TRIP8bnano is significantly shifted to hyperpolarized voltages compared to the control in rabbit SAN myocytes.
source: Figure 5B shows that the averaged If activation curve measured in presence of TRIP8bnano is significantly shifted to hyperpolarized voltages compared to the control.
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TRIP8bnano is displacing the binding of endogenous cAMP to native HCN channels in rabbit SAN myocytes.
source: This indicates that the peptide is displacing the binding of endogenous cAMP to native HCN channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the shift in the If activation curve.

claim: TRIP8bnano prevented the typical cAMP-dependent potentiation of the native If current in rabbit SAN myocytes.
source: Moreover, when the experiment was repeated in the presence of 1 µM cAMP, TRIP8bnano prevented the typical cAMP-dependent potentiation of the native If current (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TRIP8bnano significantly decreased the rate of action potential firing in single rabbit SAN cells.
source: The data in Figure 5C show that TRIP8bnano indeed significantly decreased the rate of action potential firing in single SAN cells.
evidence: This is measured by current clamp experiments as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 30% decrease in action potential rate induced by TRIP8bnano corresponds to the effect induced by physiological concentrations of acetylcholine.
source: Strikingly, the observed 30% decrease in action potential rate corresponds to the effect induced by physiological concentrations of acetylcholine (DiFrancesco et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with a cited study.

claim: The TAT sequence allows the entry of biomolecules into a cell via endocytosis and/or direct translocation across the plasma membrane.
source: Indeed, the TAT sequence allows the entry of biomolecules into a cell via endocytosis and/or direct translocation across the plasma membrane, thus leaving the cytosolic content unaltered (Guidotti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: TRIP8bnano prevented the isoproterenol-induced increase of If current density when added in the recording pipette solution in mouse SAN myocytes.
source: Strikingly, TRIP8bnano prevented the isoproterenol-induced increase of If current density, both when the peptide was added in the recording pipette solution (Figure 6A and B), and when it was used in the TAT version added to the bath (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: TAT-TRIP8bnano prevented the isoproterenol-induced increase of If current density when added to the bath in mouse SAN myocytes.
source: Strikingly, TRIP8bnano prevented the isoproterenol-induced increase of If current density, both when the peptide was added in the recording pipette solution (Figure 6A and B), and when it was used in the TAT version added to the bath (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: TRIP8bnano did not inhibit basal ICa,L in mouse SAN myocytes.
source: The specificity of TRIP8bnano for If current was confirmed by the absent inhibition of basal ICa,L (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the isoproterenol-stimulated increase of the ICaL current density between the control condition and 10 µM TRIP8bnano in mouse SAN myocytes.
source: In addition, we failed to record a significant difference in the isoproterenol-stimulated increase of the ICaL current density between the control condition and 10 µM TRIP8bnano (Figure 6E) or TAT-TRIP8bnano (Figure 6F) conditions.
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was no significant difference in the isoproterenol-stimulated increase of the ICaL current density between the control condition and 10 µM TAT-TRIP8bnano in mouse SAN myocytes.
source: In addition, we failed to record a significant difference in the isoproterenol-stimulated increase of the ICaL current density between the control condition and 10 µM TRIP8bnano (Figure 6E) or TAT-TRIP8bnano (Figure 6F) conditions.
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TAT-(SCRAMBLED)TRIP8bnano failed to significantly reduce the responsiveness of If to isoproterenol in mouse SAN myocytes.
source: We failed to observe a significant reduction in the responsiveness of If to isoproterenol in the presence of TAT- (SCRAMBLED) TRIP8bnano confirming that prevention of cAMP induced f- current stimulation was specific of the TRIP8bnano sequence.
evidence: This is measured by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prevention of cAMP induced f-current stimulation was specific of the TRIP8bnano sequence.
source: We failed to observe a significant reduction in the responsiveness of If to isoproterenol in the presence of TAT- (SCRAMBLED) TRIP8bnano confirming that prevention of cAMP induced f- current stimulation was specific of the TRIP8bnano sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between TAT-TRIP8bnano and TAT-(SCRAMBLED)TRIP8bnano.

claim: The minimal binding unit of TRIP8b, TRIP8bnano, folds in two helices upon binding.
source: The data show that the minimal binding unit of TRIP8b, TRIP8bnano, folds in two helices upon binding and suggest that this region is intrinsically disordered when it is not bound.
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis.

claim: TRIP8bnano is intrinsically disordered when it is not bound to CNBD.
source: The data show that the minimal binding unit of TRIP8b, TRIP8bnano, folds in two helices upon binding and suggest that this region is intrinsically disordered when it is not bound.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data showing limited resonance dispersion in the unbound form.

claim: The model structurally validates previous indirect evidence that TRIP8b binds to two discrete elements of the CNBD: the N-bundle loop and the C-helix.
source: The model structurally validates previous indirect evidence, which suggested that TRIP8b binds to two discrete elements of the CNBD: the N-bundle loop and the C-helix (Saponaro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a validation of previous work by the structural model.

claim: As a consequence of the interaction with TRIP8bnano, the C-helix of CNBD increases in length.
source: As a consequence of the interaction with TRIP8bnano, the C-helix of CNBD increases in length, a behavior previously observed in the case of cAMP binding (Puljung and Zagotta, 2013).
evidence: This is determined from NMR analysis and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The finding that TRIP8b and cAMP share the same binding sites on the C-helix provides a solid molecular explanation for functional data, which imply a competition between the two regulators.
source: The finding that TRIP8b and cAMP share the same binding sites on the C-helix provides a solid molecular explanation for functional data, which imply a competition between the two regulators (Han et al., 2011; DeBerg et al., 2015; Bankston et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and is consistent with previous functional studies.

claim: A direct competition model cannot fully explain the mutually antagonistic effect of TRIP8b and cAMP.
source: Another study, however, has indicated that a direct competition model cannot fully explain the mutually antagonistic effect of the two ligands (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: The inhibitory effect of TRIP8b on channel activity persists even at saturating cAMP concentrations.
source: Specifically, the fact that the inhibitory effect of TRIP8b on channel activity persists even at saturating cAMP concentrations advocated an allosteric component in the regulation mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that supports an allosteric mechanism.

claim: The N547D mutation in the N-bundle loop controls cAMP affinity in the binding pocket.
source: Our data, showing that the N547D mutation in the N-bundle loop controls cAMP affinity in the binding pocket support the conclusion that the N-bundle loop allosterically controls cAMP binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC and patch clamp experiments.

claim: The N-bundle loop allosterically controls cAMP binding.
source: Our data, showing that the N547D mutation in the N-bundle loop controls cAMP affinity in the binding pocket support the conclusion that the N-bundle loop allosterically controls cAMP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that N547D affects cAMP binding without directly contacting the cAMP binding pocket.

claim: The 37 aa long fragment identified by Lyman et al. (2017) is lacking one important contact residue, namely E240.
source: The structural model also explains why a previously identified peptide selected by Lyman et al. (2017) failed to reproduce the binding affinity of the TRIP8bcore for the CNBD. This 37 aa long fragment is lacking one important contact residue, namely E240, which, in our model, forms a salt bridge with R650 of the CNBD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and comparison with the peptide sequence from Lyman et al. (2017).

claim: The loss of E240 is presumably the reason for the major decrease in affinity (about 20 times lower) reported for the 37 aa peptide by Lyman et al. (2017).
source: The loss of one crucial interaction is presumably the reason for the major decrease in affinity (about 20 times lower) reported for this peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and the binding data from Lyman et al. (2017).

claim: TRIP8bnano binds the HCN channel CNBD with high affinity and fully abolishes the cAMP effect in all tested isoforms (HCN1, 2 and 4).
source: In functional assays, we showed that TRIP8bnano binds the HCN channel CNBD with high affinity and fully abolishes the cAMP effect in all tested isoforms (HCN1, 2 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch clamp experiments as shown in Figure 4.

claim: The polycationic TAT sequence would be best linked to the N-terminus of TRIP8bnano to avoid interference with the cationic residues of CNBD.
source: This structure suggested that the polycationic TAT sequence would be best linked to the N-terminus of TRIP8bnano to avoid interference with the cationic residues of CNBD, mainly located in the distal region of C-helix, which are crucial for the binding of the peptide.
evidence: This is a design decision based on the structural model.

claim: The TAT-TRIP8bnano peptide is efficiently delivered inside the cells.
source: From test experiments with the TAT-TRIP8bnano peptide in SAN myocytes, we can conclude that this strategy was successful in that: (i) the peptide is efficiently delivered inside the cells; (ii) it is kept in its active conformation; (iii) the TAT sequence did not damage cell membranes and did not interfere with the basic features of If and ICa,L currents; (iv) the modification did not affect the proteolytic stability of the TRIP8bnano peptide at least in the time frame of our experiments (30 min to 1 hr).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional experiments in Figure 6.

claim: TAT-TRIP8bnano is kept in its active conformation.
source: From test experiments with the TAT-TRIP8bnano peptide in SAN myocytes, we can conclude that this strategy was successful in that: (i) the peptide is efficiently delivered inside the cells; (ii) it is kept in its active conformation; (iii) the TAT sequence did not damage cell membranes and did not interfere with the basic features of If and ICa,L currents; (iv) the modification did not affect the proteolytic stability of the TRIP8bnano peptide at least in the time frame of our experiments (30 min to 1 hr).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The TAT sequence did not damage cell membranes and did not interfere with the basic features of If and ICa,L currents.
source: From test experiments with the TAT-TRIP8bnano peptide in SAN myocytes, we can conclude that this strategy was successful in that: (i) the peptide is efficiently delivered inside the cells; (ii) it is kept in its active conformation; (iii) the TAT sequence did not damage cell membranes and did not interfere with the basic features of If and ICa,L currents; (iv) the modification did not affect the proteolytic stability of the TRIP8bnano peptide at least in the time frame of our experiments (30 min to 1 hr).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The TAT modification did not affect the proteolytic stability of the TRIP8bnano peptide at least in the time frame of 30 min to 1 hr.
source: From test experiments with the TAT-TRIP8bnano peptide in SAN myocytes, we can conclude that this strategy was successful in that: (i) the peptide is efficiently delivered inside the cells; (ii) it is kept in its active conformation; (iii) the TAT sequence did not damage cell membranes and did not interfere with the basic features of If and ICa,L currents; (iv) the modification did not affect the proteolytic stability of the TRIP8bnano peptide at least in the time frame of our experiments (30 min to 1 hr).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional experiments in Figure 6 showing sustained activity over the experimental time frame.

claim: TRIP8bnano selectively controls native If currents and the rate of spontaneous firing in SAN myocytes.
source: In conclusion, we successfully used the miniaturized TRIP8bnano peptide to selectively control native If currents and the rate of spontaneous firing in SAN myocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional experiments in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: Unlike channel blockers, TRIP8bnano only interferes with the cAMP-based regulation of HCN channels, while leaving basal HCN functions unaltered.
source: Unlike channel blockers, which inhibit ionic currents, the peptide only interferes with the cAMP-based regulation of HCN channels, while leaving basal HCN functions unaltered.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional experiments showing that TRIP8bnano prevents cAMP effects without affecting basal channel properties.

claim: TRIP8bnano is selective for HCN and does not interfere with other cAMP-modulated channels present in the SAN, such as L-type Ca2+ channels.
source: In addition and in contrast to even the most selective blockers, it is selective for HCN and it does not interfere with other cAMP-modulated channels present in the SAN, such as L-type Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional experiments in Figure 6 showing no effect on ICa,L.

claim: TRIP8bnano is a promising tool in targeted therapeutic interventions.
source: Collectively, this makes TRIP8bnano a promising tool in targeted therapeutic interventions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.
